intro.title: Functional requirements: what we're building
script: Before I draw anything I want to agree on **what Ticketmaster does** for this design. The core journey is short: a fan **finds an event**, looks at the **seat map**, **grabs some seats**, and **pays** for them. Everything interesting comes from doing that for the wrong number of people at the wrong moment.

cards.title: Browse events
lines: Event pages: date, venue, lineup, prices
Browse by city, date and category
script: Fans can **browse** event pages (date, venue, lineup, price range).

cards.title: Search
lines: By artist, venue, city, date range
script: They can also **search** by artist, venue, city or date.

cards.title: Seat map
script: On an event they see a **seat map** showing which seats are available, held by someone else, or sold.

cards.title: Reserve seats
script: They can **reserve** specific seats or ask for "best available", and those seats are **held for about ten minutes** while they check out.

cards.title: Checkout
lines: Every seat is sold exactly once
script: If they **pay** in that window, the seats are theirs, and the invariant I care most about is that **a seat is sold exactly once**.

cards.title: Hold expiry
lines: Abandoned holds release on their own
Seats go straight back on sale
script: If they walk away, the hold **expires on its own** and the seats go back on sale.

cards.title: Virtual waiting room
lines: and admit them at a controlled rate
script: For hot on-sales, where demand dwarfs supply, we put fans in a **virtual waiting room** and let them into the purchase flow at a controlled rate.

cards.title: Tickets & orders
lines: Mobile ticket with a QR code
script: Afterwards they get a **mobile ticket** and can see their order history.

cards.title: Notifications
script: They also receive **notifications**: the order confirmation, and "it's your turn" when they reach the front of the queue.

outOfScope.title: Out of scope
script: I'm leaving out **resale**, which is a whole marketplace of its own, plus dynamic pricing, the tools organizers and venues use to set up events, and the scanners at the gate. Bot detection matters, but I'll treat it as a service we call. The same goes for the internals of the payment processor.
lines: Resale / secondary marketplace  ·  Dynamic pricing  ·  Organizer & venue admin tools  ·  Gate scanning hardware
Bot-detection internals (we call a service)  ·  Payment-processor internals  ·  Recommendations

intro.title: Non-functional requirements
script: Now the qualities the system needs.

cards.title: Never double-sell
script: The number-one quality is **correctness of inventory**: we **never sell the same seat twice**. That needs **strong consistency** on seats and orders.

cards.title: Spiky on-sales
lines: Quiet most of the time, then
script: The second defining quality is that traffic is **wildly spiky**. When a stadium tour goes on sale at 10 a.m., **ten million fans** show up in minutes for maybe **50,000 seats**.

cards.title: Read-heavy
lines: Browse may be a bit stale
script: The workload is **read-heavy**: roughly a hundred browses for every purchase. Beyond seats and orders, everything else (event pages, search results, even the seat map) can be **a few seconds stale**, and we'll exploit that heavily.

cards.title: Latency
script: For latency, browse and search should be **under 200 ms**, and grabbing a seat should feel instant, **under half a second** even at peak.

cards.title: Availability
script: Browse needs **four nines**. For the purchase path I'd rather **degrade gracefully**: under overload, put people in a queue rather than throw errors.

cards.title: Fairness
script: Because so many people are disappointed, the process has to **feel fair**: roughly first come, first served, with bots not getting ahead.

cards.title: Durability
script: Orders and payments must be **durable**, and charging a card must be **idempotent**.

cards.title: Fresh seat map
lines: At most a few seconds stale
script: The **seat map** may lag, but only by a few seconds: a seat someone just took should vanish quickly, or fans keep clicking on seats they can't have.

cards.title: Scale
script: On **scale**, I'll assume about **100 million users**, a million tickets sold a day, and around 100,000 events on sale at any time.

estimates.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
script: On a normal day, with about **a million tickets** sold across 100,000 events, that's roughly **12 orders a second** and a couple of thousand browse requests a second. That's a modest system. A hot on-sale is different: that's 200 people per seat. If each of them refreshes the seat map every five seconds, that's about **2 million requests a second** on one event, three orders of magnitude above normal.
The interesting thing about the storage math is how **small** it is. A billion seat rows at a couple of hundred bytes is about **200 GB**, and orders add a couple of GB a day.

takeaway.title: Takeaway: stop the crowd, protect the inventory
script: Data volume isn't the problem. **Contention** is: 200 people reaching for the same row. So two things will shape the design. We stop the crowd **before** it reaches the inventory. And the inventory itself uses **conditional writes** on a strongly consistent store, partitioned by event.
takeaway.heading: Takeaway: a small, fought-over inventory behind a huge, mostly disappointed crowd
lines: 200 fans per seat and 2M req/s → stop the crowd at the edge, and admit buyers only as fast as checkout can serve them
Only ~200 GB of seats, but every one is contested → conditional writes on a strongly consistent store, sharded by event

slides.title: Start with the simplest thing that works
script: Let's start with the **simplest system that could possibly sell a ticket**: fans on the web or in the app, talking over HTTPS to **one server**.
The API is small.

slides.title: The API
script: **GET /events** and **GET /events/{id}** for browsing. **GET /events/{id}/seats** returns the seat map. **POST /holds** takes an event and a list of seats (or "best available, quantity 4") and returns a hold with an expiry time. **POST /orders** takes a hold ID and payment details and turns the hold into tickets. Last, **GET /orders** lists my tickets.

rows: the seat map: available · held · sold
event + seats (or best available ×4) → hold + expiry

slides.title: Why not buy in one step?
script: Splitting **hold** from **order** is the first important design decision, and it comes straight from the product. Checkout takes minutes: you type your card number, maybe fumble a 3-D Secure prompt. We can't ask the fan to pay first and only then find out whether the seat is still there. And we can't block every other buyer while one person types.

items.detail: typing a card number, a 3-D Secure prompt

items.text: Pay first? The seat may be **gone** by the time you finish
items.detail: and now we owe you a refund

items.text: Lock the seat while you pay? **Everyone else waits**
items.detail: one slow typist blocks every other buyer

slides.title: Reserve first, pay second
script: So we **reserve first, pay second**, with a time limit in between. Most of the rest of this design is about making that two-step dance correct and keeping it fast under load.
This one box is fine for a small venue's box office. It obviously has no durability yet, so let's fix that first.

slides.title: A relational database
script: The server gets a **database**, and I'd pick a relational one, **Postgres**, without much hesitation. The thing we must get right is "two people cannot buy the same seat". That's a textbook job for **transactions and conditional updates**. And as we just computed, the data is small enough that we don't need a NoSQL store for volume.

slides.title: The data model
script: The core tables: **Venue** holds the physical layout, meaning sections, rows and seat coordinates for drawing the map. **Event** is a performer at a venue on a date, with an on-sale time. **Seat** (or event-seat) is the inventory row: one per seat *per event*, carrying the price tier and a **status**: AVAILABLE, HELD or SOLD. A held seat also carries a **hold_id** and a **hold_expires_at**. **Order** records who bought what and the payment reference, and **Ticket** links an order to each seat it bought.

slides.title: Layout vs. inventory
script: One thing worth calling out: the **layout** and the **inventory** are different kinds of data. The layout is big (an arena map has tens of thousands of seat shapes) but it almost never changes, and it's identical for every event at that venue. The inventory is tiny per seat, a status and a price, but it changes constantly during an on-sale. Keeping them apart lets us cache the layout forever and treat the inventory very differently.

rows: big: tens of thousands of seat shapes
same for every event at the venue
one row per seat per event

slides.title: General admission
script: For general-admission events with no assigned seats, the same model works with a counter per price tier instead of a row per seat. I'll focus on reserved seating because it's the harder case.

slides.title: Split the read path from the write path
script: The monolith is about to be pulled in two very different directions, so I'll split it along the line that matters most: **reads versus writes**.

slides.title: The Event Service: the read path
script: The **Event Service** owns the catalog: events, venues, performers, and the seat-map layout. It's almost entirely reads, it's tolerant of staleness, and it gets the 100-to-1 share of traffic. We'll put caches and a CDN in front of it and scale it horizontally without thinking very hard.

slides.title: The Booking Service: the write path
script: The **Booking Service** owns the **inventory**: it returns the current availability for an event and it places holds. Its traffic is much lower on a normal day, but it's the part that must be **strongly consistent**, and it's the part that gets hammered during an on-sale. Keeping it separate means we can scale, deploy and protect it on its own. A bad deploy to the event pages shouldn't stop people from buying, and a meltdown during an on-sale shouldn't take down browsing for every other event.

rows: a few seconds stale is fine

slides.title: An API gateway in front
script: In front of both is an **API gateway**. It terminates TLS, authenticates the user, applies **rate limits** per user and per IP, and routes each request to the right service. It will also become the enforcement point for the waiting room later on, so it's worth having from the start.

items.text: **Rate limits** per user and per IP
**Routes** each request to the right service

items.detail: the one place every booking call passes through

slides.title: One shared database, for now
script: Both services still share one Postgres for now. That's fine. The booking side's tables are the ones that matter, and we'll come back to how they're partitioned.

slides.title: Two fans, one seat
script: Now the heart of the problem: two fans click the same seat at the same moment. How does the Booking Service make sure exactly one of them gets it?

slides.title: The naive version: read, then write
script: The naive version is "read the seat, see it's available, write HELD". That's a classic race: both requests read AVAILABLE and both write HELD.

steps.note: both fans think they hold seat 14C

slides.title: One atomic conditional update
script: Instead we do it in **one atomic conditional update**: *set status to HELD, with my hold ID and an expiry ten minutes out, where the seat ID is in my list and the seat is available (or its old hold has expired)*. Then we check the row count. If I asked for four seats and four rows changed, I have them all.

slides.title: The database arbitrates
script: If fewer changed, someone beat me to one, so I roll back the transaction and tell the user to pick again. The database's row locking does the arbitration. No distributed lock, no read-then-write gap.

items.text: **All rows changed** → the hold is yours
items.detail: 4 seats asked, 4 rows updated

items.text: **Fewer rows** → roll back, ask the fan to pick again
items.detail: someone beat you to at least one seat
the second update waits, then sees HELD

slides.title: Lazy expiry and the sweeper
script: Notice the **expiry is lazy**. A HELD seat whose **hold_expires_at** is in the past already counts as available for the next hold, so correctness never depends on a background job running on time. We still add a **Hold Expiry Worker** that sweeps every few seconds and flips lapsed holds back to AVAILABLE. That keeps the seat map honest and produces a "seats released" event we'll use later.

slides.title: Holds in Postgres or in Redis?
script: The popular alternative is to keep holds in **Redis** with a TTL, using SET-if-not-exists per seat, and write to Postgres only on purchase. It's faster and expiry is free, but now the truth about a seat lives in **two places**. You need careful handling when Redis says "held" and Postgres says "sold", or when a Redis failover forgets holds.

rows: truth in two places; failover can forget holds

slides.title: One source of truth
script: Because the waiting room will cap how many people hit this path, Postgres can easily handle the hold rate. So I prefer one source of truth. If we ever needed more, Redis would be a fine optimization in front of it, not a replacement.

items.text: The waiting room **caps the hold rate**
items.detail: Postgres handles it easily

items.text: **One source of truth** for every seat
Redis later, if needed: **in front of** Postgres
items.detail: an optimization, not a replacement

slides.title: Checkout: pay, then confirm, exactly once
script: The **Order Service** turns a hold into a purchase, and it's where money meets inventory, so the ordering of steps matters.
When the fan submits payment, we first create an **order in PENDING state** tied to the hold ID.

slides.title: Authorize, sell, capture
script: Then we ask the **payment provider** to **authorize** the card, which reserves the funds without moving them. Only once that succeeds do we run the second conditional update: *set status to SOLD where the seats carry my hold ID*, in the same transaction that marks the order CONFIRMED and writes the tickets. If that update touches all the seats, we **capture** the payment.

slides.title: When the hold was lost
script: If it doesn't (say the hold expired and someone else got a seat), we **void the authorization** and apologize. The fan is never charged for seats they don't have, and a seat never ends up sold to two people.

steps.label: sorry: a seat was lost, no charge

slides.title: Idempotent at every step
script: Every step is **idempotent**. The client sends an idempotency key with the order. We pass our order ID to the provider as its idempotency key, so a retried request or a double-clicked "Buy" never charges twice.

items.text: Client → us: an **idempotency key** per order
items.detail: a retry or a double-click finds the same order

items.text: Us → provider: **our order ID** as its key
items.detail: a retried authorize never charges twice
PENDING → CONFIRMED, never backwards

slides.title: Webhooks and reconciliation
script: Payment providers also confirm asynchronously through **webhooks**, and the webhook handler is just another idempotent "advance this order's state" call. A small reconciliation job compares our PENDING orders with the provider's records, to catch anything that fell between the cracks.

slides.title: A little grace at checkout
script: One product detail: we give checkout a little **grace**. If the fan submitted payment before their hold expired, we treat the hold as still valid while the authorization is in flight. The seats aren't released mid-payment. Holds have a hard deadline for starting checkout, not for finishing it.

items.text: Paid **before** the hold expired → hold stays valid
items.detail: while the authorization is in flight

items.text: The deadline is for **starting** checkout, not finishing it

slides.title: Search with a dedicated index
script: Fans rarely navigate to an event by ID. They type "taylor swft chicago" and expect the right result. A SQL **LIKE** query doesn't do typo tolerance, relevance ranking or faceted filters, and it would put browse load on the same database that guards our inventory. So search gets its own **Search Service** on top of an **Elasticsearch** index.

slides.title: The search document
script: Each document is an event, denormalized: performer names and aliases, venue, city, geo-point, date, category, price range, and a coarse "on sale / sold out" flag. That supports full-text matching with fuzziness, filters like "this weekend, within 50 km", and ranking that blends text relevance with popularity.

slides.title: Feeding the index: CDC, not dual writes
script: The index is fed by **change data capture** from the primary database. Every insert or update to an event is streamed out of the Postgres write-ahead log and applied to the index. That's better than having the Event Service "dual-write" to both, because dual writes drift apart whenever one of them fails. CDC means the database stays the source of truth, and the index catches up a second or two later.

rows: Event Service writes DB, then index
stream the Postgres WAL into the index
index catches up; DB stays the truth

slides.title: Search is a little behind, on purpose
script: That lag is fine for search. It would **not** be fine for seat availability, which is why the search index only carries a coarse sold-out flag, never seat-level inventory. Clicking through to an event always gets live availability from the Booking Service.

slides.title: Cache event pages and seat-map snapshots
script: Next, a **Redis cache tier** in front of the database for the two hottest reads.

The first is **event details and venue layouts**. They're read constantly and change rarely, so the Event Service caches them with a long TTL and invalidates on update. Layouts in particular can be cached almost forever: they're versioned, and the venue for a given event doesn't change.

slides.title: The most expensive read
script: The second, more interesting one is the **seat-map availability snapshot**. Without a cache, every fan looking at the seat map runs a query over thousands of seat rows. During an on-sale that's the single most expensive read we have, and it competes directly with the writes that sell tickets.

slides.title: A compact snapshot per event
script: Instead the Booking Service keeps a **compact snapshot per event**: a bitmap or a small per-section count of available seats. It's rebuilt from the database at most every second or two, and every fan's seat-map request is served from it. A stadium's worth of seat statuses fits in a few kilobytes as a bitmap, so this is cheap to store and cheap to ship.

slides.title: Cache for reads, database for decisions
script: The trade-off is that the map can be **a second or two stale**, so a fan might click a seat that was just taken. That's fine, because the map is only a **hint**. The authoritative check is the conditional update when they try to hold it. If that fails we say "sorry, someone just grabbed that one" and refresh their map. **Cache for reads, database for decisions** is the rule throughout.

steps.label: someone just grabbed it · fresh map

slides.title: Push the read path to the edge with a CDN
script: Even with a cache, every request still reaches our gateway and services. The next step is a **CDN** in front of everything.

slides.title: What the CDN caches
script: Static assets are the obvious part: the JavaScript bundle, images, and the **venue map geometry**, which can be served as a long-cached, versioned file. The bigger win is **event pages and their JSON**. An event page is the same for everyone, so the CDN can cache it for tens of seconds and absorb nearly all the browse traffic at edge locations close to the fans. Only misses go back to the **origin**, which is our API gateway.

rows: the same for everyone; most browse traffic

slides.title: One origin request per edge per second
script: Personalized or inventory-sensitive calls (holds, orders, "my tickets") are marked uncacheable and pass straight through. Even the seat-map snapshot can sit at the edge with a one-second TTL if we need to. Ten million fans hitting it then turns into one origin request per edge location per second.

slides.title: Built for the shape of an on-sale
script: The CDN also gives us something we'll lean on in a moment: a huge, globally distributed tier that is very good at **serving the same bytes to millions of people**. It handles that cheaply, and it can soak up attack traffic before it ever reaches us. That's exactly the shape of traffic a hot on-sale produces.

items.text: Great at **the same bytes to millions** of people
items.detail: and cheap at it

items.text: **Soaks up attack traffic** before it reaches us
Exactly the shape of a **hot on-sale**
items.detail: we'll lean on it for the waiting room

slides.title: The on-sale problem
script: So far the design handles a normal day comfortably. Now it's 9:59 a.m. and **ten million fans** are hovering over the "Buy" button for a 50,000-seat show.
Think about what happens without protection.

slides.title: The thundering herd
script: At 10:00 everyone requests the seat map and tries to hold seats. Caches help with the map, but **holds are writes** on the same few thousand rows, so the conditional updates fail for 199 out of 200 people. Those 199 immediately retry. Load on the Booking Service and its database shard goes vertical, latency spikes for the few who *could* succeed, and timeouts cause more retries. That's a **thundering herd**, and the usual outcome is that the site falls over and nobody buys anything.

steps.label: conditional updates on the same rows

steps.note: site falls over · nobody buys anything

slides.title: Why more hardware doesn't help
script: Scaling the database further doesn't help. The contention is on the **same rows**, so throwing hardware at it buys little, and it's pointless anyway: no matter how much capacity we add, only 50,000 seats exist. Most of those requests are **destined to fail**. The right move is to stop them before they start.

items.detail: more machines don't make one row less contested

items.text: Only **50,000 seats** exist, whatever the capacity

slides.title: The virtual waiting room
script: That's the **virtual waiting room**. For an event flagged as high-demand, fans who arrive don't get the seat map, they get a place in **line**, kept in a **Queue Store**. We admit people from the front of the line into the purchase flow **at the rate the booking path can actually serve**, typically a few thousand a minute.

slides.title: A steady, bounded stream of shoppers
script: Everyone else waits on a cheap page that tells them their position. The rest of the system then only ever sees a steady, bounded stream of real shoppers. Let's zoom into how that works.

slides.title: Waiting room: joining the line
script: Zooming in. When a fan opens a high-demand event, the edge serves a static **waiting page** instead of the event, and the page calls the **Waiting Room Service** to **join** the queue.

slides.title: Joining is one ZADD
script: Joining is a single **ZADD** into a Redis **sorted set** for that event, keyed by a queue ticket ID with a score that sets the order. The service returns the fan's ticket ID and their position, signed so it can't be tampered with.

slides.title: Why a sorted set
script: Sorted sets give us O(log N) inserts and "what's my rank" lookups, and ten million entries is only a few hundred megabytes. One Redis primary per hot event, with a replica, handles it comfortably. If needed we can shard the line into buckets.

items.text: If needed, **shard the line into buckets**

slides.title: The score decides the order
script: The interesting choice is **the score**. For people who arrive **after** the on-sale starts, it's simply arrival time: first come, first served. But for the people who showed up early and sat in the **pre-sale lobby**, arrival order mostly measures who has the fastest connection or the most aggressive script.

items.text: Arrive **after** the start: score = arrival time
items.detail: first come, first served

items.text: Arrive **early**, in the pre-sale lobby: arrival order is noise
items.detail: it measures connection speed and how aggressive your script is

slides.title: Randomize the lobby
script: So at the start time we give everyone in the lobby a **random** position, then append later arrivals behind them. That's what Ticketmaster and Queue-it do, and it's both fairer and kinder to the system. Nobody gains anything by hammering refresh at 9:59:59.

rows: fast connections and scripts gain nothing

slides.title: Join once, cheaply
script: Joining happens **once** per fan, so even ten million joins spread over a few minutes is tens of thousands of writes per second. That's well within a Redis node. The repeated traffic, "am I there yet?", is the part we must keep away from this service.

slides.title: Waiting cheaply: status from the edge
script: Ten million people waiting means ten million browsers asking **"where am I now?"**. If each asks the Waiting Room Service every few seconds, we've just rebuilt the thundering herd one layer earlier.
The trick is to make the answer **the same for everyone**.

slides.title: Per fan vs. per event
script: Each fan already knows their own queue number; it's in the signed ticket they got when they joined. The only thing that changes is a single global value per event: **"now serving number N"**, plus an estimated admission rate. We publish that as a tiny **Queue Status** object. The page polls it through the **CDN** with a one-second cache TTL, and works out "you're 48,210th in line, about 14 minutes" locally.

slides.title: Polls answered at the edge
script: Now ten million polls per few seconds become, at the origin, **one request per edge location per second**. The CDN serves identical bytes to everyone, which is the job it's best at.

slides.title: Poll the edge, don't push
script: We could push updates over WebSockets instead, but holding ten million open connections for a queue that changes once a second is far more expensive than letting the CDN answer polls. We'd add a little jitter to poll intervals so clients don't synchronize.

rows: one origin hit per edge per second
instant, for a value that moves once a second

slides.title: Waiting has to be almost free
script: This is the key insight of the whole waiting room. **Waiting has to be almost free**, because nearly everyone does it and most of them will leave without tickets. We only pay real cost for the small number of people at the front of the line.

items.detail: 10M fans, 50,000 seats
a static page and a cached number

items.text: Real cost only for **the front of the line**

slides.title: Admission control: how fast to let people in
script: Something has to decide how fast "now serving" advances. That's the **Admission Controller**, and it's essentially a feedback loop.

slides.title: Capacity signals
script: The naive version is a fixed rate, say 2,000 fans per minute. The better version watches **capacity signals** from the booking path: how many admitted shoppers are currently active, Booking Service and database latency, hold failure rates, and how many seats are left.

bullets.heading: Capacity signals from the booking path

items.detail: admitted fans who are still shopping
Booking Service and database p99

slides.title: The feedback loop
script: It advances N to keep the number of **concurrent shoppers** near a target. If p99 latency on holds starts climbing, it slows down. When shoppers finish or time out, it lets more in. It's the same idea as TCP congestion control, pointed at a database shard.

slides.title: Sizing the target
script: A useful rule of thumb for the target: with ~50,000 seats, ~4 tickets per order and a 10-minute hold window, the booking path never needs more than a few tens of thousands of concurrent shoppers. That's a number we can load-test ahead of the on-sale, rather than guessing what ten million people will do.

rows: a few tens of thousands, at most

slides.title: The endgame
script: Seats left also drives the **endgame**. As inventory runs out we admit fewer people. When everything is sold or held, we stop admitting and flip the status to **"sold out, but holds may still release"**. When it's truly gone, we tell everyone still in line *now*, instead of letting them wait an hour for nothing. Being honest early is a big part of making the experience feel fair.

rows: sold out, but holds may still release

slides.title: The controller fails safe
script: The controller is a single small process per event, with a standby. If it dies, "now serving" just stops advancing for a few seconds, which fails safe.

items.text: **One small process per event**, with a standby
If it dies, **now serving stops advancing**
items.detail: for a few seconds, until the standby takes over
nobody is admitted who shouldn't be

slides.title: Access tokens: making the line enforceable
script: A queue is only real if you **can't skip it**. Anyone can read our JavaScript and call the hold API directly, so the line must be enforced server-side.

slides.title: Claim a token, then book
script: When a fan's page sees that "now serving" has passed their number, it **claims** admission from the Waiting Room Service. The service checks their ticket against the current N and issues a short-lived, signed **access token**: a JWT carrying the event ID, the user ID, and an expiry of maybe 15 minutes. Every booking call then goes through the **API Gateway**, which **verifies the token's signature locally**.

slides.title: The access token
script: No database lookup, no call back to the waiting room, so verification costs microseconds even at peak. Requests for a protected event without a valid token are bounced to the waiting page.

slides.title: No sharing, no hoarding
script: Tokens are bound to the user and the event, so sharing one doesn't help. The Booking Service can also cap holds per token, which stops one admitted user from hoarding the whole floor. When the token expires the shopper's slot frees up, and that shows up in the capacity signals, so the controller admits the next person.

items.detail: a shared token is useless to anyone else
one admitted user can't hoard the whole floor
capacity signals see it, and the next fan is admitted

slides.title: A hard bound on booking traffic
script: This also gives the Booking Service a **hard guarantee**. Its traffic during an on-sale is bounded by the number of live tokens, not by the size of the crowd. That's what lets us keep simple, correct Postgres conditional updates for holds instead of reaching for something exotic. The waiting room isn't just a UX feature. It's what makes the core design viable.

slides.title: Bots, fairness and verified fans
script: The last piece of the waiting room is keeping the line **human**. Scalpers run thousands of bots to grab inventory and resell it, and every spot a bot takes is a real fan who leaves empty-handed.
The cheapest place to stop bots is **at join time**, before they hold a spot.

slides.title: Screen at the door, not the till
script: The edge calls a **bot defense** service (device fingerprinting, IP reputation, behavioral signals, a challenge when things look suspicious). I'm not designing it, but where it sits matters: in front of the queue, not in front of checkout, where the damage would already be done.

columns: Cost of a bot that slips through
rows: none yet: it never gets a spot in line
it already took a spot, and maybe held seats

slides.title: Identity and Verified Fan
script: The second layer is **identity**. We allow **one queue spot per verified account** (and per payment card at checkout), so a thousand browser tabs don't buy a thousand chances. For the biggest tours, Ticketmaster's "Verified Fan" goes further: fans **register days in advance**, get screened offline, and receive access codes for a specific on-sale. That turns an unbounded crowd into a known, pre-vetted list, so you can even size the on-sale before it starts.

slides.title: Each check in the cheapest place
script: Everything else is rate limits at the gateway, per-token hold caps, and order limits per event. None of it is perfect; this is an arms race. But the architecture puts each check in the cheapest place it can go, and keeps the expensive inventory path reserved for people who've already passed all of them. That's the end of the deep dive, so let's zoom back out.

slides.title: An event bus for everything after the sale
script: Back to the full system. Plenty of things need to happen **because** seats were held, released or sold, and none of them should slow down checkout. The confirmation email, issuing the mobile ticket, updating search's sold-out flag, analytics, payouts to promoters. So we put an **event bus**, Kafka, behind the database.

slides.title: Why not just publish after commit?
script: The important detail is **how** events get onto it. If the Order Service committed to Postgres and then published to Kafka, a crash between the two would lose the event, or publish one for a transaction that rolled back.

steps.note: seats sold, but no email, no ticket

slides.title: The transactional outbox
script: Instead we use the **transactional outbox** pattern. The same transaction that marks seats SOLD also inserts an "OrderConfirmed" row into an outbox table, and a relay (or CDC on the outbox) publishes it to Kafka. An event exists if and only if the state change committed.

slides.title: Delivery guarantees
script: Consumers are idempotent, since delivery is at-least-once. Topics are **partitioned by event ID**, so all changes for one show stay in order.

slides.title: Notifications and tickets
script: The first consumer is the **Notification Service**. On OrderConfirmed it generates the tickets and sends the confirmation through third-party email and push providers.

slides.title: Rotating QR codes and a buffer
script: Mobile tickets use a **rotating QR code**: the barcode is derived from a secret plus the current time, so a screenshot stops working after a few seconds, which kills a lot of ticket fraud. The same service sends the "it's your turn" push for fans who left the waiting page.
Because this all hangs off the bus, a slow email provider never delays a purchase. It just builds a backlog that drains when the provider recovers.

slides.title: A live seat map with server-sent events
script: Admitted shoppers are staring at the seat map deciding what to buy, and nothing is more frustrating than clicking seat after seat that's already gone. A one-or-two second snapshot is OK, but we can do better for the people who are actually shopping.
The **Seat Map Stream** service consumes **SeatsHeld, SeatsReleased and SeatsSold** events from Kafka and pushes them to clients over **server-sent events**.

slides.title: Snapshot plus deltas
script: A client loads the snapshot, opens a stream for that event, and applies the deltas as they arrive. Seats grey out within a fraction of a second of someone else grabbing them. When the expiry worker frees a lapsed hold, those seats light back up. Each delta carries a sequence number, so a client that misses some just re-fetches the snapshot.

slides.title: Why server-sent events
script: I chose **SSE over WebSockets** because the traffic is one-way, server to client. SSE is plain HTTP, it works through proxies and the CDN, and browsers reconnect automatically. Polling would also work, but at a one-second interval it's a lot of wasted requests, and it's still less fresh.

rows: plain HTTP, proxies and CDN, auto-reconnect

slides.title: Push only where it changes the outcome
script: Here the waiting room pays off again. Live streams only go to the **admitted** shoppers, maybe tens of thousands per hot event, not ten million. That's a few stream servers, each fanning one Kafka partition out to many connections. Fans still in line, or browsing low-demand events, keep using the cached snapshot. Push is something we give to the people for whom freshness actually changes the outcome.

rows: tens of thousands per hot event

slides.title: Partitioning inventory by event
script: Two scaling questions remain: how the inventory database grows, and what happens across regions.

The inventory **shards by event ID**. Every query on the hot path ("availability for event X", "hold these seats at event X", "sell this hold") is scoped to a single event, so every transaction stays on **one shard**, with no distributed transactions. An event's seats, holds and the orders that touch them all live together.

slides.title: Hot partitions
script: The catch is **hot partitions**: one event can be a million times hotter than its neighbours. So we know the big on-sales in advance and **place them deliberately**, moving a mega-event onto a dedicated shard before its on-sale, with replicas for the read side. Because the waiting room bounds the write rate, a single well-provisioned Postgres primary per hot event is plenty.

slides.title: Going multi-region
script: For regions, I'd split along the same consistency line as before. The **catalog** (events, venues, search) is replicated asynchronously to **every region**, so browsing is local and fast everywhere.

slides.title: One home region per event
script: Each event's **inventory has a single home region**, normally the one closest to the venue, and every hold and sale for it is written there. That costs an extra hundred milliseconds or so for a fan buying a ticket on another continent. In exchange, we never have to reconcile two regions that both sold seat 14C. For a ticketing system that's an easy trade.

slides.title: When a home region fails
script: If a home region fails, its events' inventory fails over to a standby replica in another region, with a brief pause in sales for those events. We'd rather pause than risk double-selling.

slides.title: The complete system
script: Here's the whole design. Let's walk one hot on-sale through it end to end.

Fans load the event through the **CDN**, which serves the page, the venue map, and for a high-demand show, the **waiting page**. They **join the queue** once, through the Waiting Room into a Redis **sorted set**, with randomized order for early arrivals. Then they wait, cheaply, polling a **cached "now serving" number** at the edge. An admission controller advances that number as fast as the booking path can handle, and each admitted fan claims a **signed access token** that the gateway checks on every booking call.

Inside, the **Booking Service** serves the seat map from a cached snapshot, with **live deltas over SSE**. It places **holds** with a single conditional update on the event's **Postgres shard**, where holds expire lazily and a sweeper releases lapsed ones. The **Order Service** authorizes payment, flips held seats to SOLD only if the hold is still theirs, captures, and writes an **outbox** event, all idempotently. **Kafka** carries those events to notifications, ticket issuance, the live seat map and analytics. Browsing and search run on caches, a CDN and an Elasticsearch index fed by CDC, replicated to every region, while each event's inventory lives in exactly one home region.

The two big ideas: first, **protect a tiny, contended inventory with a strongly consistent store and conditional writes**. Use one source of truth, make the cache a hint and the database the decision. Second, **shape the crowd before it reaches that store**. Make waiting almost free, admit people at the rate we can serve, and enforce it with tokens. If I had more time I'd go deeper on general-admission inventory, the resale marketplace, and load-testing an on-sale before it happens. But this is the system I'd ship.
